h1: Handling noise complaints from neighbours of a brewpub
title: Handling Brewpub Noise Complaints | Craft Beer School
desc: How a brewpub can prevent and handle noise complaints from neighbours, from India's noise limits to sound checks, closing routines and plant noise.
teaser: One unhappy neighbour can cost a brewpub its late licence. Most noise complaints are preventable.
standfirst: Music, crowds and rooftop chillers all make noise. Neighbours notice. Repeated complaints can bring police visits or trouble at licence renewal. This guide covers how to prevent them and what to do when one arrives.
sections: Know the limits that apply to your site

India's noise rules set permitted ambient levels by zone. Residential areas are limited to 55 dB(A) by day and 45 dB(A) at night. Commercial areas are allowed 65 dB(A) by day and 55 dB(A) at night. Night time runs from 10 pm to 6 am. Silence zones around hospitals, schools and courts are stricter still. Loudspeakers and amplified music at night are tightly restricted, with any relaxations decided by state and local authorities.

A brewpub on a commercial street with flats above or behind it sits between those numbers. Check the zoning of your site and of the nearest homes. Then check the current local rules on amplified music hours, which change and differ between cities.
The noise is usually not the band

Founders think of noise as music. Complaints are often about other things:

  • Rooftop plant: condensing units, glycol chillers and extract fans running all night.
  • Guests leaving at closing time, talking in the car park and slamming car doors.
  • Bottle bins emptied late at night or early in the morning.
  • Keg and malt deliveries at 6 am.
  • Smokers gathered outside a side entrance under bedroom windows.

A glycol chiller cycling on and off at 2 am is more irritating to a light sleeper than a band that stopped at 10:30. Ask your refrigeration supplier for the sound rating of the outdoor units and place them away from the nearest windows, with acoustic screening if needed.

A basic sound level meter costs little next to a licence problem. Use it on a busy night at the boundary of your site and at the nearest home's side of the street, at the hours that matter: 9 pm, 10 pm and closing. Log the readings. A record of regular measurement helps you make your case if a complaint reaches the police or the licensing authority.

Set a house limit for indoor music and fix the amplifier so staff cannot push it past that level on a Saturday. A limiter on the sound system works better than a rule on the wall.

Remember how decibels add up. Every 10 dB increase sounds roughly twice as loud to the human ear. A room at 85 dB(A) is not slightly louder than one at 75 dB(A). To a neighbour it sounds about twice as loud. Turning the music down by a few decibels at 10 pm is often enough to stop the calls. Guests inside rarely notice the change once conversation fills the room.
Build sound control into the fit out

Most noise leaks through the weakest point: doors, windows and roof openings. Lobbied entrances with two sets of doors, sealed glazing on the side facing homes and acoustic lining in the ceiling all cut leakage. Place speakers away from external walls and angle them into the room. Keep live music in the part of the venue furthest from residents.

These choices are cheap during fit out and expensive after. If you are planning outdoor tables, read our guide on outdoor seating permission first, because the terrace is often where complaints begin.

The best complaint is one that never needs to be made. Introduce yourself to the residents' association and the nearest households before you open. Give them a direct phone number for the duty manager. People who can call you are less likely to call the police.

Invite them to the soft opening. Tell them when deliveries will arrive and when the venue closes. If you host a late event, warn them in advance. Neighbours who feel informed are far more tolerant than neighbours who feel ignored.

Treat every complaint seriously, even one you think is unfair. A simple routine works:

  1. Thank the person and take the details: date, time and what they heard.
  2. Check your own logs and meter readings for that time.
  3. Fix what you can straight away, whether that is the music level, the bin time or the chiller position.
  4. Call them back to say what you changed.

Keep a complaints register. Patterns show up quickly: the same night of the week, the same event or the same delivery driver.
Make quiet part of the closing routine

Closing time is when a lot of noise happens. Lower the music in the last half hour. Ask guests to keep voices down outside. Help them book cabs from inside, which is also the responsible thing to do for anyone who has been drinking. Move bottle bins at a sensible hour.

Neighbour relations affect revenue as well as reputation, because a late licence lost is trading hours lost. The Brewery Business Management course covers site selection, licensing and operations together. Start this week by measuring your noise at the nearest home at 10 pm on your busiest night.
faqs: What are the noise limits for a brewpub in India?
Limits depend on the zone. Residential areas allow 55 dB(A) by day and 45 dB(A) at night. Commercial areas allow 65 dB(A) and 55 dB(A). Check local rules on amplified music hours.
What causes most noise complaints at brewpubs?
Often not the music but rooftop plant, guests leaving at closing time, bottle bins and early deliveries.
How should a brewpub respond to a noise complaint?
Take the details, check your own logs, fix what you can and call the neighbour back to explain what changed.
